title: Chicken Stock in Dal Makhani? A Former MasterChef Judge Just Ignited Indian Food's Loudest Fight
excerpt: George Calombaris's Instagram reel adding chicken stock cubes to dal makhani has reignited the perennial debate over who gets to reinterpret Indian classics — and where the red line sits.
body:
Few dishes carry the emotional weight of dal makhani. The slow-cooked Punjabi staple — a patient marriage of whole black lentils, butter, cream, and time — is a litmus test in Indian kitchens. Restaurants are judged by it. Weddings are remembered by it. And now, thanks to a viral Instagram reel, the internet is fighting over it.

Former MasterChef Australia judge George Calombaris recently posted his "version" of dal makhani, and the backlash was swift. The Greek-Australian chef's recipe swapped out the dish's long, slow simmer for a 25-minute shortcut and, most controversially, added chicken stock cubes to what is traditionally a vegetarian dish.

"Today we're going to cook my version, and I'll repeat, my version of dal makhani," Calombaris said in the reel, pre-empting the criticism he clearly anticipated. It did not help.

## The Sacred and the Stock Cube

The criticism was not merely about taste. For many viewers, the addition of chicken stock to dal makhani crossed a cultural and religious line. Dal makhani is a vegetarian dish in a tradition where vegetarianism is often rooted in faith, not fashion.

"You have a lot of non-vegetarian food already. Why alter an authentic vegetarian dish by using chicken stock?" one Instagram commenter wrote. Another was blunter: "Chicken Stock!!!! It's clearly a recipe for hardcore non-vegetarians… You've changed it too much; perhaps you should rename it, as it is not dal makhani in any way."

Celebrity chef Gautam Kumar weighed in more diplomatically, noting that dal makhani is often the dish by which customers judge an entire Indian restaurant. "Its significance in shaping a restaurant's reputation cannot be overstated," Kumar said, underscoring why the dish inspires such protective instincts.

## A Pattern, Not an Incident

Calombaris is far from the first Western chef to stumble into this territory. The controversy echoes past flare-ups — from the infamous 2018 "crispy rendang" debacle on MasterChef UK, where judges eliminated a Malaysian-born contestant for not making her rendang crunchy, to ongoing debates over British supermarkets selling "curry" as a catch-all for everything from korma to vindaloo.

What makes the dal makhani episode sting, many argue, is the gap between acknowledgement and accountability. Calombaris admitted his version was "not authentic," yet still called it dal makhani — a name that carries centuries of culinary identity. For critics, the issue is not experimentation itself, but the casual borrowing of a dish's name while stripping its soul.

## The Diaspora's Double Bind

For Indian Americans and NRIs watching from abroad, the controversy hits differently. Many in the diaspora have spent years advocating for Indian cuisine to be taken seriously in Western markets — pushing past the "curry house" stereotype toward recognition of the country's staggering regional diversity. Dishes like dal makhani, butter chicken, and biryani have become bridges between cultures.

But there is a tension: the very mainstreaming that NRIs champion can also lead to the kind of casual reinterpretation that strips a dish of its meaning. When a Western celebrity chef treats a vegetarian classic as a blank canvas for chicken stock, it raises uncomfortable questions about who profits from Indian food's global rise, and who controls the narrative.

## Where the Line Sits

The debate is unlikely to resolve neatly. Indian cuisine has always evolved — the tomato in today's curries was a Portuguese import, and the chilli that defines so much Indian cooking arrived barely 500 years ago. Innovation is part of the tradition.

But there is a difference between evolution from within and appropriation from without. When Ranveer Brar experiments with dal makhani, he does so as an inheritor of the tradition. When a MasterChef judge adds chicken stock and calls it by the same name, many feel the gesture is less creativity than carelessness.

For now, Calombaris's reel continues to rack up comments. The dal makhani endures — slow-cooked, unapologetic, and apparently not in the mood for shortcuts.
